name: Elena Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the business reporter at a regional daily paper, which in practice means the port, the two big factories on the ring road and whichever shop chain is closing this month. My day starts with company results and the shipping figures, then calls, then usually a visit somewhere, a warehouse or a trade fair or a café with someone from a union. I write two or three stories a day for the website and the print edition. I like it when a boring set of accounts hides a real story, like a factory quietly moving work abroad. What wears me out is being asked to make every story shorter and faster.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Marco, who's a civil engineer on the new tram line. We rent, but I own half a small flat my aunt left me and I rent that out, so there's a bit of income from that. I've got well over six months of costs saved. The paper pays better than most around here, and there are other papers and business magazines in the city if I ever needed to move. I don't use AI tools at all. I don't need the newest gadget. I need the dock workers to keep returning my calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, each with a name. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me, to be honest. I've never seen it do anything I couldn't do better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, which is what I've been saying for two years. At work I'd tell people to stop worrying about chatbots and worry about the paper's sale instead. I wouldn't post much online, I rarely do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be uneasy. We were bought by a bigger group in the spring, and they're cutting costs everywhere. Even if AI fizzles, the paper still has new owners who measure reporters in clicks per hour. I'm average at the job, not a star, so that's my real worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work well. I'd keep saving and keep the rental flat. I'd probably update my contacts with the business magazine in the city, just in case the group closes the business desk. I wouldn't touch AI, there'd be no reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a low hum of worry about the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the low hum feel like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the Monday morning email with the traffic figures for every reporter. My stories about the port do well in print but not online. Every Monday I look at the list and see my name near the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the business desk closed, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go to the business magazine, or into communications for the port. The port press office has asked me twice. I'd lose some independence, but I'd keep the pay.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, as I've said for two years.
I'd tell colleagues to worry about the **paper's sale**, not chatbots.
think: I think the **new owners** measuring clicks are my real worry.
I'm **average**, so the Monday traffic list puts me near the bottom.
do: Keep my head down and **do the work well**.
Keep saving and keep the **rental flat** income.
Refresh contacts at the **business magazine** in case the desk closes.
feel: I feel **mostly fine**, with a low hum of worry about the owners.
S0.quote: Even if AI fizzles, the paper still has new owners who measure reporters in clicks per hour.
fieldNote: Her unease comes from the **recent sale** of the paper, not AI.
The Monday **traffic list** is a concrete weekly pressure.
She has a fallback offer from the **port press office**.
She doesn't post online; she keeps a **low profile**.

steps.text: Keep covering the port and ring road factories as normal
Keep saving and keep renting out the inherited flat
Wait to see if the new owners close the business desk

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more real, I'll admit. The group already sends us summaries made by software from company results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, let the machine do the results summaries, but someone has to go to the port. I'd say it to my editor in those words. Online I'd stay quiet. With friends I'd probably say journalism has had worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it hits me harder than I'd like. A lot of my day is turning company reports into short stories, and that's exactly the writing and checking the card talks about. A press release about the port's profits takes software ten seconds. Getting the port's union rep to admit the night shift is being cut takes me three weeks of coffees. The question is whether the owners pay for the three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the port more and do fewer results stories, so my work looks different from what the software makes. I'd take the port press office seriously and have a proper conversation with them within six months. I'd save more, maybe stop the holiday budget. I still wouldn't use the tools unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Like the ground getting a little softer every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You won't use the tools even if colleagues do. Doesn't that put you behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'm not going to beat software at writing summaries, so why try? My bet is on the bits it can't do. If that bet's wrong, I'll go to the port office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would say I'm being stubborn, and that engineers use software all day. Marco also says the tram line will need people on site for years. Between the two of us, I'm the exposed one, and we both know it.

say: I'd tell my editor: let the machine do summaries, but someone must **go to the port**.
I'd stay **quiet online** and say journalism has had worse.
think: I think it hits me hard; **results stories** are exactly what software does.
The question is whether the owners pay for **three weeks of coffees**.
do: Spend more time **at the port** and write fewer results stories.
Have a proper talk with the **port press office** within six months.
Cut the **holiday budget** and save more.
feel: I feel **uncomfortable**, like the ground getting softer every month.
S1.quote: A press release about the port's profits takes software ten seconds. Getting the port's union rep to admit the night shift is being cut takes me three weeks of coffees.
fieldNote: She sees much of her day as **exposed summary work**.
She bets on **source work** rather than learning the tools.
She admits she is **the exposed one** compared with Marco.
The **port press office** is a real fallback she'd pursue.

steps.text: Visit the port weekly and drop routine company results stories
Meet the port press office about a communications job within six months
Cut the holiday budget this year and save the difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then I'd be out of a job before I'm thirty. That's my gut reaction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say the government and the companies both need to slow down. I'd say it calmly, because shouting doesn't help. At work I'd ask management straight out what their plan is for the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the paper would replace most reporters in that first year. Business news is numbers and writing, and the card says AI does that better and cheaper. The robots arriving three years later doesn't help a reporter at all. My only edge is people, and the owners might not care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write my CV the same night, and I've never written one in a panic before. I'd go to the port office and anyone else who'd talk to me in the first month. I'd stop all spending that isn't bills and keep the rental income as a safety net. And I'd talk to Marco about whether we should buy a place now, while his job is steady, or wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A cold, clear kind of alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say the port job is your fallback. Wouldn't communications get hit too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Press releases are writing as well. I suppose I'd be hoping the port wants someone who knows the people. But I'd be lying if I said I had a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the rental flat, does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a lot. The rent covers about a third of my share of bills. If I had to, I could sell my half, but it's the one thing my aunt left me and I'd hate that.

say: I'd say government and firms both need to **slow down**.
I'd ask management straight out what their **plan for staff** is.
think: I think the paper replaces **most reporters** in the first year.
My only edge is **people**, and the owners might not care.
do: Write my **CV** the same night and contact the port office.
Stop all spending except **bills**; keep the rental income.
Decide with Marco whether to **buy a place** now or wait.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, a cold and clear kind of alarm.
S2.quote: I'd write my CV the same night, and I've never written one in a panic before.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** within a year of AGI.
She admits her **port fallback** is also exposed.
The **rental flat** cushions her, but selling it feels like betrayal.
She stays **calm in tone** while expecting the worst.

steps.text: Rewrite the CV and contact the port press office within a month
Stop all spending except bills and rent
Decide with Marco whether to buy a home while his job is steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to see it coming. Not enough time to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be sensible: training schemes, help for people moving jobs. At work I'd say the same. I'm not one for big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three or four more years in business reporting, then it'd fade. I'd be thirty-one or thirty-two. My partner says I should learn the tools. I'd rather learn a job the tools can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in something practical, maybe surveying, because Marco's world needs it and it's half outdoors. The robots would come three years after the AI, so that buys more time than writing ever would. I'd keep reporting while I studied. And I'd keep saving and keep the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier. At least there's a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Surveying is quite a jump. What draws you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, watching Marco's lot on the tram line. They're outside, measuring, arguing with contractors. It's not glamorous, but somebody has to stand on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of leaving journalism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the contacts I've built. Five years of coffees with dockers and union reps. That doesn't move with you into a new trade.

say: I'd call for **training schemes** and help for people moving jobs.
I'd say it **sensibly**, without big speeches.
think: I think I'd have **three or four years** before reporting fades.
I'd rather learn a job the tools **can't do**.
do: Start a **part-time surveying course** while still reporting on the port.
Keep saving every month and keep renting out the **inherited flat**.
Choose a trade with the **robot lag** in mind, outdoors and hands-on.
feel: I feel **anxious but steadier**; at least there's a road.
S3.quote: My partner says I should learn the tools. I'd rather learn a job the tools can't do.
fieldNote: Five years lets her plan a move into **hands-on surveying**.
She uses the **robot lag** deliberately when choosing a new trade.
She refuses to learn AI tools even with **time to adapt**.
Losing her **contacts** is the hardest part for her.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time land surveying course
Keep saving and keep renting out the inherited flat
Keep reporting on the port while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I could be a completely different person in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so governments and businesses should plan. Nothing dramatic. At work, I'd say let's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd be tempted to do nothing, and I know that's the dangerous part. I'd tell myself I've got years, then suddenly it's 2034. I think I'd still have to leave reporting before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting for five or six years and save hard. I'd set myself a deadline, say 2031, to start retraining, and write it on the calendar. I'd probably look at surveying again, or property management, since I already rent out a flat. And I'd keep the port press office as a contact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the background. It's quiet, but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a deadline on the calendar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know myself. I don't like change, and I'll put it off until it's forced on me. A written date is the only thing that works with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Property management: where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the flat my aunt left. I deal with the tenants, the boiler, the letting agent. It's small, but it's people and buildings, and those don't disappear overnight.

say: I'd say there's time, so governments and firms should **plan calmly**.
At work I'd say **let's not panic**.
think: I'd be **tempted to do nothing**, and that's the danger.
I think I'd still have to **leave reporting** before it lands.
do: Report for **five or six years** and save hard.
Write a **2031 retraining deadline** on the calendar.
Look at **surveying or property management** as next careers.
feel: I feel **quietly anxious**, in the background, all the time.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd be tempted to do nothing, and I know that's the dangerous part.
fieldNote: She knows her **resistance to change** is her real risk with ten years.
She sets a **written deadline** to force herself to act.
Her **rental flat** suggests property management as a path.
Even with a decade, she expects to **leave reporting**.

steps.text: Save hard over five or six more years of reporting
Start a surveying or property management course by 2031
Keep reporting and wait until the 2031 deadline to switch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to do what I'm slow at, which is change. What would help is a proper redundancy deal and help paying for a practical course, something like surveying, while I still have an income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how readers feel. People in this city trust a name they recognise in the paper. I don't know if they'd trust a machine's name, or if they'd even notice.

headlineQuote: I don't need the newest gadget. I need the dock workers to keep returning my calls.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old business reporter** at a regional daily covering the port and factories.
She **never uses AI** and bets on sources and face-to-face reporting.
A **rental flat** from her aunt and solid savings give her a cushion.
She is uneasy even in a quiet world because of **new owners**, and alarmed by fast AGI.
With time she plans a move into **surveying**, but fears her own **slowness to change**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to change, which she's slow at.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **redundancy deal** and help paying for a **practical course** while still earning.
